title: How Presidential Pardons Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how presidential pardons work. They open with personal news (a baby born to Josh's future sister-in-law) and a note that President Obama had not yet acted on clemency requests, with only two Thanksgiving turkeys pardoned. The main discussion covers the checks-and-balances context, notable controversial pardons (Ford pardoning Nixon, Bush commuting Scooter Libby, Clinton pardoning Mark Rich), and what a pardon does (restores civil rights, does not erase the record) versus other forms of clemency: commutation, remission, respite, and conditional pardons. They cover the English royal prerogative origins, the impeachment exception, the Taft-era contempt of Congress loophole, the Supreme Court ruling that a pardon can be refused except in capital cases, and the history of blanket pardons (Washington's Whiskey Rebellion, Kennedy's 1956 narcotics pardons, Harding freeing Eugene Debs-era Espionage Act prisoners, Ford and Tokyo Rose, Carter and draft dodgers, Lincoln and Arthur O'Brien). They close with pardon statistics by president, the Office of the Pardon Attorney, and a live trivia event pitch.

segments.title: Opening banter and Obama's clemency inaction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with personal news about a new baby and a birthday party, then discuss President Obama not yet acting on clemency requests and the two Thanksgiving turkeys he pardoned, plus the origin of the turkey pardon tradition.

segments.title: Pardons and checks and balances
segments.summary: The hosts frame the presidential pardon as the one power outside the checks and balances system and note how it has become a political tool that generates public anger.

segments.title: Controversial pardons: Ford, Libby, Clinton and Mark Rich
segments.summary: They discuss Ford's pardon of Nixon before charges, Bush's commutation for Scooter Libby, and Clinton's conditional pardon of Mark Rich, including the Rich-Kunstler-Libby connection and the Rich pardon's effect on the Eric Holder nomination.

segments.title: What a pardon does and types of clemency
segments.summary: Chuck explains that a pardon ends prison time and restores civil rights lost after a felony, but the record remains. He defines clemency as the umbrella term and distinguishes pardon, commutation, remission, and respite.

segments.title: Limits of pardon power and its English origins
segments.summary: They cover what a pardon cannot do, including impeachment and civil obligations, its roots in English royal prerogative, and the Constitution's Hamilton-era debate over including it.

segments.title: Contempt of court loophole, refusing pardons, and the O.J. example
segments.summary: They explain why a pardon covers only offenses against the United States, how Taft's ruling gave Congress a contempt power, the Supreme Court ruling that a pardon can be refused except in capital cases, and the O.J. Simpson civil suit example.

segments.title: History of blanket pardons and famous cases
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh recount Washington's Whiskey Rebellion amnesty, Kennedy's 1956 narcotics pardons, Harding's Espionage Act pardons and Eugene Debs, Ford's Tokyo Rose pardon, Carter's pardon of draft dodgers, Carter's commutation of Patty Hearst, and Lincoln's pardon of Arthur O'Brien.

segments.title: Office of the Pardon Attorney and pardon statistics
segments.summary: They describe the Office of the Pardon Attorney's role in reviewing petitions and giving recommendations, then go through pardon counts by president, noting Roosevelt's total, Truman's percentage, and the recent Carter, Reagan, Clinton, and Bush numbers.

segments.title: Trivia night pitch and housekeeping
segments.summary: Chuck pitches a planned all-star trivia event in Atlanta around Dragon Con and thanks listeners who helped with an iPhone download issue.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode with a listener mail call-out and the standard sign-off.
